hmmt-feb-2026-comb-01.title: Count topic sequences
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-01.body:
The condition uses up three of the four questions on A, C, G; the fourth topic is either a repeat of A, C or G, or is N.
- Fourth topic N: all four topics distinct: $4!=24$ sequences.
- Fourth topic a repeat (say two A's): $\frac{4!}{2!}=12$ sequences, for each of the $3$ choices: $36$.

Probability $\frac{24}{24+36}=\frac25$.

**Answer: $\frac25$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-01.title: Inclusion–exclusion
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-01.body:
Sequences in $\{A,C,G,N\}^4$ containing $A$, $C$, $G$: $4^4-3\cdot3^4+3\cdot2^4-1=256-243+48-1=60$. Among those, the ones with no $N$ are surjections onto $\{A,C,G\}$: $3^4-3\cdot2^4+3=36$. So $60-36=24$ contain $N$, probability $\frac{24}{60}=\frac25$.

**Answer: $\frac25$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-02.title: Linearity over faces
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-02.body:
Face $i$ contributes $i$ if it is rolled at least once in the $4$ rolls, otherwise $0$. It is never rolled with probability $\left(\frac34\right)^4=\frac{81}{256}$. So the expected score is
$$(1+2+3+4)\left(1-\frac{81}{256}\right)=10\cdot\frac{175}{256}=\frac{875}{128}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{875}{128}$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-02.title: Enumerate
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-02.body:
Averaging the final score over all $4^4=256$ equally likely roll sequences (adding each face's label only the first time it appears) gives $\frac{1750}{256}=\frac{875}{128}$.

**Answer: $\frac{875}{128}$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-03.title: Which numbers must cross 4
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-03.body:
Every number that starts on the wrong side of $4$ (larger to its left, or smaller to its right) must be swapped with $4$ at some point, and conversely we can sort each side separately without touching $4$ once those crossings are done. So we need at most one "wrong-side" number.
- None: $1,2,3$ left of $4$ and $5,6,7$ right, any orders: $3!\cdot3!=36$.
- Exactly one: choose the misplaced number ($6$ ways); then one side of $4$ holds a fixed set of $4$ numbers and the other $2$, in any order: $6\cdot4!\cdot2!=288$. (For instance, if $5$ is left of $4$, the left side is $\{1,2,3,5\}$ with $5$ adjacent to $4$ after sorting the left side, and a single swap moves it across.)

Total $36+288=324$.

**Answer: 324**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-03.title: Brute force
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-03.body:
Counting permutations of $1..7$ in which at most one pair $(x,4)$ is an inversion (i.e. $x>4$ before $4$ or $x<4$ after it) gives $324$.

**Answer: 324**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-04.title: Multiply expected factors
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-04.body:
Before the $n$th break there are $n$ sticks, and the red stick is chosen with probability $\frac1n$, in which case its length halves. So its expected length is multiplied by $\frac1n\cdot\frac12+\frac{n-1}n=\frac{2n-1}{2n}$, independent of its current length. After $5$ minutes:
$$\frac12\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac56\cdot\frac78\cdot\frac9{10}=\frac{945}{3840}=\frac{63}{256}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{63}{256}$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-04.title: Exhaustive enumeration
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-04.body:
Recursively averaging over all $1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4\cdot5=120$ equally likely choice sequences gives exactly $\frac{63}{256}$ $\left(=\binom{10}5/2^{10}\right)$.

**Answer: $\frac{63}{256}$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-05.title: Staircases in a grid
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-05.body:
Put $2^a5^b$ ($0\le a,b\le9$) in column $a$, row $b$ of a $10\times10$ grid. The second condition means $T$ is a "staircase": in each column it is the bottom $h_a$ cells, with $h_0\ge h_1\ge\cdots\ge h_9$. The first condition ($2^a5^b\leftrightarrow2^{9-a}5^{9-b}$) says exactly $h_a+h_{9-a}=10$ for each $a$.

So $h_0,\dots,h_4$ determine everything, with $h_5=10-h_4\le h_4$, i.e. $10\ge h_0\ge\cdots\ge h_4\ge5$. The number of nonincreasing $5$-tuples from $\{5,\dots,10\}$ (six values) is $\binom{5+5}{5}=252$.

**Answer: 252**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-05.title: Enumerate staircases
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-05.body:
Listing all nonincreasing height sequences $(h_0,\dots,h_9)$ with values in $0..10$ and checking $h_a+h_{9-a}=10$ by computer gives $252$.

**Answer: 252**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-06.title: Halve the payments instead
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-06.body:
Instead of doubling the debt, halve the payments: on day $i=0,1,2,\dots$ he pays $(1+b_i)2^{-i}$ of the original debt, with independent fair bits $b_i$. He becomes debt-free iff
$$\sum_{i\ge0}(1+b_i)2^{-i}\ge\pi\iff\sum_{i\ge0}b_i2^{-i}\ge\pi-2.$$
(If the sum reaches $\pi$ only in the limit, that is a measure-zero event.) $\sum b_i2^{-i}=b_0.b_1b_2\ldots$ in binary is uniform on $[0,2]$, so the probability is $\frac{2-(\pi-2)}2=\frac{4-\pi}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{4-\pi}{2}$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-06.title: Simulation
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-06.body:
Simulating two million debt histories for $60$ days gives a debt-free frequency of about $0.4295$, matching $\frac{4-\pi}2\approx0.4292$.

**Answer: $\frac{4-\pi}{2}$**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-07.title: Edge cases, then parallel chords
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-07.body:
Let $A,B$ be the two bases.

**Edge cases** (one base entirely on one side): $\emptyset$, all $20$, $A$, $B$; $M\supseteq A$ with $1$–$9$ vertices of $B$ forming a consecutive run ($9\cdot10=90$); similarly $90$ with $B$ and part of $A$; and the complements of these $180$. Total $4+180+180=364$.

**Main case.** Otherwise the plane cuts both decagons, along parallel lines $\ell_1$ (in $A$'s plane) and $\ell_2$ (in $B$'s plane); conversely any two parallel lines come from a plane. Projecting $B$ onto $A$, we count pairs $(X,Y)$ of vertex sets of one decagon cut off (on corresponding sides) by parallel lines, with $1\le|X|,|Y|\le9$.

Each set is a run of consecutive vertices on an arc of the circumcircle. If $\ell_1$ meets the circle at $P_1,P_2$ and $\ell_2$ at $Q_1,Q_2$, the arcs $P_1Q_1$ and $P_2Q_2$ have equal measure (parallel chords cut equal arcs). Hence the numbers of decagon vertices on these two arcs differ by at most $1$.

Say $|X|=x\ge y=|Y|$ and $X=\{A_1,\dots,A_x\}$. If $x-y=2k$ is even, $Y$ must drop $k$ vertices from each end: $1$ choice. If $x-y=2k-1$ is odd, it drops $k-1$ and $k$ in some order: $2$ choices. Among $x,y\in\{1,\dots,9\}$, there are $5^2+4^2=41$ same-parity pairs and $40$ opposite-parity pairs, and $10$ rotations of $X$: $10(41+80)=1210$.

Total $364+1210=1574$.

**Answer: 1574**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-07.title: Computer check
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-07.body:
Place the prism at height $1$ over a unit-circumradius decagon. For each of $2$ million random unit normals $n$, sort the vertices by $n\cdot v$; every proper prefix is a set cut off by a plane. Collecting all prefixes and their complements, plus $\emptyset$ and the full set, yields exactly $1574$ distinct sets.

**Answer: 1574**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-08.title: Pair each point with its reflection
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-08.body:
$|S|=1+6+12+18+24=61$. Triangles with the centre $O$ as a vertex never count, so use the other $60$ points, which form $30$ antipodal pairs $\{P,P'\}$.

Take three pairs $\{P,P'\},\{Q,Q'\},\{R,R'\}$ on three distinct lines through $O$. Label so that $P,Q,R$ lie in angular order in a half-plane. Of the $8$ triangles using one point from each pair, exactly two contain $O$ strictly inside: $PQ'R$ and $P'QR'$. A triangle with two vertices on one line through $O$ never contains $O$ strictly (or is degenerate). So the answer is $2\times$(number of choices of $3$ pairs on distinct lines through $O$).

Lines through $O$ with more than one pair: the $3$ lines through opposite vertices carry $4$ pairs each (distances $1,2,3,4$), and the $3$ lines through opposite edge-midpoints carry $2$ pairs each (points at distances $\sqrt3$ and $2\sqrt3$ from $O$); every other line through $O$ carries one pair. Bad triples:
- two pairs on an edge-midpoint line: $3\binom22\cdot28=84$;
- exactly two on a vertex line: $3\binom42\cdot26=468$;
- three on a vertex line: $3\binom43=12$.

Answer: $2\left(\binom{30}3-564\right)=2(4060-564)=6992$.

**Answer: 6992**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-08.title: Brute force
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-08.body:
Generate the $61$ lattice points in coordinates and test all $\binom{61}3=35990$ triples: nondegenerate ones with $O$ strictly inside (all three orientation tests the same strict sign) number $6992$.

**Answer: 6992**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-09.title: Structure: $A_n$ is a disjoint union of blocks of size $\varphi(d)$
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-09.body:
$|A_i|=i$ (take $j=i$); if $i\mid j$ then $|A_i\cap A_j|=i$, so $A_i\subseteq A_j$; and $A_{\gcd(i,j)}\subseteq A_i\cap A_j$ with equal sizes, so $A_i\cap A_j=A_{\gcd(i,j)}$.

Let $B_n=A_n\setminus\bigcup_{k<n}A_k$ (pairwise disjoint). Then $A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n}B_d$: elements of $B_d$ with $d\mid n$ are in $A_n$; and if $k\nmid n$, $A_n\cap B_k\subseteq A_{\gcd(n,k)}$ with $\gcd(n,k)<k$, which is disjoint from $B_k$. So $n=\sum_{d\mid n}|B_d|$, forcing $|B_n|=\varphi(n)$ (Möbius inversion / induction).

For $d\mid250$, $\max A_d\ge\max B_d$, and the eight sets $B_1,B_2,B_5,B_{10},B_{25},B_{50},B_{125},B_{250}$ have sizes $1,1,4,4,20,20,100,100$ and are disjoint. For disjoint sets of given sizes, $\sum\max$ is minimised by filling them with consecutive blocks of $1,2,3,\dots$ in increasing order of size (an exchange argument: the set holding the overall largest element can be taken to be the largest one, then induct). That gives maxima $1,2,6,10,30,50,150,250$, total $499$.

Construction: $B_1=\{1\}$, $B_2=\{2\}$, $B_5=\{3..6\}$, $B_{10}=\{7..10\}$, $B_{25}=\{11..30\}$, $B_{50}=\{31..50\}$, $B_{125}=\{51..150\}$, $B_{250}=\{151..250\}$, and $A_n=\bigcup_{d\mid n}B_d$ (other $B_d$ use fresh large numbers). Then $\max A_d=\max B_d$ for each $d\mid250$ (e.g. $A_{125}=B_1\cup B_5\cup B_{25}\cup B_{125}$ has max $150$), and the sum is $499$.

**Answer: 499**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-10.title: Hamiltonian paths on a cylinder
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-10.body:
Think of $S$ as a $20\times3$ grid wrapped around a cylinder in the $x$-direction: each step moves up or down by one row, or one column to the right (cyclically). We count Hamiltonian paths from the top row to the bottom row. By rotational symmetry, fix the start at $(0,2)$ and multiply by $20$.

Structure (following the official solution). Along the top row the path consists of a *head* (an initial horizontal run), then alternating *valleys* (dips below the top row and back) and *hills* (horizontal runs on top), until it leaves the top row for good at a point $C$; the part of the path from just below $C$ to the point $E$ where it last leaves row $1$ forms a similar "ridge" in rows $0$–$1$; after that the path is forced. One shows:
- every valley has width $1$ (otherwise a top-row vertex is isolated) and depth $1$ (a depth-$2$ valley propagates forced moves that eventually strand a vertex);
- hills on the top ridge have odd length, hills on the lower ridge have length $1$;
- the heads have odd length, and once the two ridges are chosen the rest of the path is determined.

If the top head has length $19-2k$, the rest of the top ridge is a composition of $2k$ into even parts: $1$ way if $k=0$, $2^{k-1}$ ways if $k\ge1$. The lower ridge has length $19-2k$ and splits as an odd head plus parts of length $2$: $10-k$ ways. Total
$$10+\sum_{k=1}^{9}(10-k)2^{k-1}=10+\sum_{j=0}^{8}(9-j)2^j=10+(2^{10}-11)=1023.$$
So the answer is $20\cdot1023=20460$.

**Answer: 20460**

hmmt-feb-2026-comb-10.title: Brute force on smaller cylinders
hmmt-feb-2026-comb-10.body:
The same count for a $W\times3$ cylinder (even $W$) is $W\left(2^{W/2}-1\right)$; a depth-first search counting Hamiltonian paths for $W=4,6,8,10,12$ gives $12, 42, 120, 310, 756$, matching. For $W=20$ this is $20\cdot1023=20460$.

**Answer: 20460**
